sentences: In the middle of a dark room, under hard light, two men are locked in a fight.
Below the ring, the faces of the spectators are packed close together.
This is Stag at Sharkey's, painted in 1909 by the American artist George Bellows.
Bellows was born in Columbus, Ohio, in 1882.
At Ohio State University he played baseball and basketball.
In 1904 he left college for New York, where he studied painting with Robert Henri.
He soon became the leading young member of the Ashcan School, a group of artists who painted everyday life in the city.
Near his studio was a saloon run by Tom Sharkey, a former heavyweight boxer and Navy veteran.
In the back room, Sharkey kept a boxing ring.
At the time, public boxing matches were against the law in New York.
So the fights were staged as private club events, open only to members.
A fighter from outside was given a temporary membership for the night, and such a fighter was called a stag.
The title of the painting comes from this custom.
Now look at the two boxers in the center.
Their heads meet, and their bodies are tangled into a single shape.
They stand out like silhouettes against the black background, lit by harsh electric light.
Bellows used quick brushstrokes that blur the edges, so the bodies seem to move.
A referee stands with the fighters as well.
Next, look down at the edge of the ring at the bottom of the picture.
The heads of the spectators are right in front of us.
The point of view is low, so we seem to stand among the crowd, looking up at the ring.
The composition is often seen as a return to the triangle he had used in Club Night, painted two years earlier.
The paint is laid on thickly, and the brushstrokes are left in plain view.
Bellows is said to have claimed he knew nothing about boxing.
He was simply painting "two men trying to kill each other."
In those years, people were divided about boxing.
Some called it crude and brutal, while supporters such as Theodore Roosevelt saw it as a healthy expression of manliness.
Later, Bellows made a lithograph of the same scene.
The painting entered the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1922 and has stayed there ever since.
Bellows died in 1925, at the age of forty-two, after his appendix burst.
Now step back and take in the whole picture.
The two lit bodies and the crowd in the shadows make a single scene.
Imagine yourself standing among the spectators below the ring.
What would you feel?
